title: Teenagers With Friends Watching
text:
Parents often worry about teenagers driving with friends in the car, and statistics on crashes suggest they have reason to. Margo Gardner and Laurence Steinberg at Temple University in Philadelphia wanted to see the effect of peers on risk taking directly.

They recruited three age groups: young adolescents, college-age youths and adults. Each person played a computer driving game called Chicken. A car moved along a road toward an intersection, and at some point a traffic light turned yellow. The longer the player kept driving, the more points they earned, but if the light turned red and a wall appeared before they stopped, the car crashed and they lost the points for that round. Each participant also filled out questionnaires about risky choices.

Half of the participants played alone. The other half came with two friends of the same age, who sat in the room and watched, and could offer advice.

The presence of friends made a large difference for the youngest group. Adolescents with peers watching took substantially more risks in the game than adolescents playing alone. The effect was smaller for the college-age group and very small for adults. The same pattern appeared in the questionnaires. Later brain-imaging work by Steinberg's team suggested that the presence of peers heightens activity in teenagers' reward systems.
lesson: Teenagers are not simply reckless; they are especially sensitive to their friends. Expect more risk when peers are present and plan for it together.
source: Gardner, M., and Steinberg, L. (2005). Peer influence on risk taking, risk preference, and risky decision making in adolescence and adulthood: An experimental study. Developmental Psychology, 41(4), 625-635.
